questions.stem: According to the current classification, the living world is divided into three major domains. These are:
options: Viruses
Eukaryotes
Archaea
Eubacteria
questions.explanation: The three domains are Eukaryotes, Eubacteria and Archaea. Viruses are not cells (no cytoplasm, no nucleus, no metabolism) and are treated separately.

questions.stem: About the nuclear envelope of the eukaryotic cell:
options: It consists of two membranes separated by a perinuclear space
Its inner membrane is in contact with the cytoplasm
Its inner membrane is separated from the chromatin by the lamina
Its pores allow substances to pass only from the nucleus to the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: The outer membrane faces the cytoplasm; the inner one is lined by the lamina on the chromatin side. Nuclear pores allow endogenous and exogenous substances to transit in both directions.

questions.stem: About the plasma membrane of the eukaryotic cell:
options: It is a lipid bilayer associated with transmembrane and peripheral proteins
Its outer and inner surfaces differ in structure and function
It contains receptors
It may present microvilli and intercellular junctions
questions.explanation: All four are stated in the course. The difference between the two surfaces is called membrane asymmetry; the main role of the membrane is to maintain the integrity of the cell.

questions.stem: Which of the following belong to the endomembrane system as described in the course?
options: Endoplasmic reticulum
Mitochondria
Golgi apparatus
Lysosomes
questions.explanation: The endomembrane system includes the ER, the Golgi apparatus and lysosomes, which communicate via vesicles budding from their membranes. Mitochondria are described separately, with their own double membrane.

questions.stem: Under the electron microscope, one region of a cell's endoplasmic reticulum carries ribosomes while another is devoid of them. Concerning these two regions:
options: The ribosome-free region synthesizes proteins destined for mitochondria
The ribosome-bearing region participates in the synthesis of proteins destined for secretion
The ribosome-free region is involved in lipid synthesis
The ribosome-free region synthesizes most membrane proteins
questions.explanation: Ribosome-bearing ER is the RER (secreted proteins and most membrane proteins); ribosome-free ER is the SER (lipid synthesis). Mitochondrial proteins are made by free ribosomes, not by the SER.

questions.stem: Which of the following proteins are synthesized by ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum rather than by free ribosomes?
options: A mitochondrial protein
A hormone secreted outside the cell
A cytosolic enzyme
A plasma membrane protein
questions.explanation: The RER makes proteins destined for secretion and most membrane proteins. Free ribosomes make proteins for the cytosol and for organelles such as peroxisomes and mitochondria.

questions.stem: About the Golgi apparatus:
options: It modifies, sorts, packages and distributes the products synthesized by the ER
It consists of a stack of flattened sacs (dictyosomes) associated with vesicles
It is involved in glycosylation
It is the main distributor of newly synthesized membranes
questions.explanation: All four statements come directly from the course's description of the Golgi apparatus.

questions.stem: A cell is treated with a drug that inhibits all its hydrolases. Which organelle's function is most directly impaired?
options: Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Mitochondria
Lysosomes
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing hydrolases able to degrade most endogenous and exogenous molecules. The Golgi handles glycosylation and sorting, the SER lipid synthesis.

questions.stem: About mitochondria:
options: The inner membrane is more permeable than the outer membrane
The respiratory chain is located in the matrix, next to mitochondrial DNA
They are bounded by a double membrane whose outer membrane is highly permeable
The cristae contain the respiratory chain and the ATP-synthesizing machinery
questions.explanation: The outer membrane is highly permeable and the inner one less permeable; its invaginations (cristae) carry the respiratory chain and ATP synthesis. The matrix holds mitochondrial DNA and protein-synthesis components, not the respiratory chain.

questions.stem: About the general organization of the bacterial cell (Eubacteria):
options: The nucleoid is separated from the cytoplasm by an envelope
The cell wall is mainly composed of peptidoglycan
The cytoplasm is poor in proteins and devoid of ribosomes
The chromosome consists of several linear filaments located at the periphery of the cell
questions.explanation: The resistant cell wall is mainly peptidoglycan. The chromosome (nucleoid) is a single closed-loop filament in the center of the cell, not separated from the cytoplasm, which is rich in proteins and contains ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures may be present in some bacteria but are not constant?
options: A polysaccharidic capsule
A plasma membrane
Plasmids
Pili and flagella
questions.explanation: Capsule, inclusions, pili, flagella and plasmids are listed as structures eubacteria may possess. Every bacterium is bounded by a plasma membrane.

questions.stem: About archaea:
options: They possess several linear chromosomes, like eukaryotes
Formerly called archaebacteria, they are unicellular microorganisms
They are much larger than eubacteria, measuring 10–100 µm
They divide by binary fission and often possess proteinaceous flagella
questions.explanation: Archaea have a size range similar to eubacteria (0.1–15 µm) and a single circular chromosome. They divide by binary fission and often move with proteinaceous flagella.

questions.stem: At the molecular level, archaea:
options: Are much closer to eukaryotes than to eubacteria
Share with eukaryotes some proteins that are absent from eubacteria
Have DNA replication, repair and transcription proteins that resemble eukaryotic proteins
Have information-processing proteins that are mostly similar to bacterial ones
questions.explanation: Archaea resemble eubacteria in morphology and metabolism, but molecularly (especially information-processing proteins) they are far closer to eukaryotes.

questions.stem: A unicellular organism is isolated from an acidic hot spring. Its envelope contains no peptidoglycan but a protein layer covering the plasma membrane, and its membrane phospholipids are isoprenoid ethers. This organism is most likely:
options: A eubacterium
A eukaryote
An archaeon
A virus
questions.explanation: No peptidoglycan, a protein envelope and isoprenoid ether lipids are unique to archaea. Eubacteria have peptidoglycan walls and, like eukaryotes, fatty acid ester phospholipids.

questions.stem: About the envelope and membrane lipids of archaea:
options: Their phospholipids are isoprenoid ethers derived from a long-chain alcohol
Their phospholipids are fatty acid esters, as in eubacteria
Their envelope contains peptidoglycan, as in most eubacteria
Their envelope is generally a protein layer covering the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Archaeal phospholipids are isoprenoid ethers, unlike the fatty acid esters of eubacteria and eukaryotes, and their envelope is a protein layer without peptidoglycan.

questions.stem: About the habitats of archaea:
options: Some thrive in anaerobic, highly saline or very hot conditions
They colonize deep-sea hydrothermal vents, saline waters and acidic hot springs
Some live in the intestines and lungs of mammals
Many live in common habitats such as soils, lakes and oceans
questions.explanation: Archaea are famous for extreme environments, but the course stresses that many live in ordinary habitats, including soils, oceans and mammalian intestines and lungs.

questions.stem: About viruses:
options: They are obligate parasites that cannot reproduce outside a host cell
They lack cytoplasm and a true nucleus
Each virion contains both DNA and RNA
Their genome is surrounded by a protein capsid
questions.explanation: A virus consists of a nucleic acid — DNA or RNA, not both — surrounded by a protective protein capsid. It has no cytoplasm, no nucleus and must infect a host cell to multiply.

questions.stem: Correctly match each virus with the nature of its genome:
options: Hepatitis B virus → DNA
SARS-CoV-2 → DNA
HIV → RNA
Tobacco mosaic virus → RNA
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B is the course's DNA virus example; HIV and SARS-CoV-2 are RNA viruses. Figure 03 shows tobacco mosaic virus with an RNA genome.

questions.stem: Concerning the multiplication cycle of a virus:
options: The virus uses its own metabolism to produce energy
The virus hijacks the host cell's machinery to replicate its genome and synthesize its proteins
Once inside the cell, the virus produces its proteins independently
New viral particles are assembled, then the virions are released from the host cell
questions.explanation: A virus has no metabolism of its own and cannot produce its proteins independently; it uses the host's machinery, then new particles are assembled and released.

questions.stem: In a culture, infected cells keep producing virions for several days without being destroyed, and the released virions are surrounded by a membrane. Concerning this mode of release:
options: It corresponds to cell lysis
It corresponds to budding
The viral envelope comes from a portion of the host cell's plasma membrane
The host cell is necessarily destroyed immediately after release
questions.explanation: In budding, enveloped viruses leave by taking a piece of plasma membrane as their envelope, and the cell may keep producing viruses for some time. In lysis, the cell is destroyed.

questions.stem: About the organization of the viral capsid (Figure 03):
options: Tobacco mosaic virus has a helical capsid
The adenovirus genome is RNA
Adenovirus has a polyhedral capsid made of capsomeres
The bacteriophage has a complex structure with a head containing DNA and a tail
questions.explanation: Figure 03 shows three capsid types: helical (tobacco mosaic virus, RNA), polyhedral (adenovirus, DNA) and complex (bacteriophage, head with DNA plus tail sheath and fibers).
